pass_b_english: They say through the voice of the one who sings as to the Lord our Jesus Christ, 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we are regarded as sheep for the slaughter' (Romans 8:36).
Therefore, we do not lose heart, but even if our outer man is being corrupted, yet the inner man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16).

It is fitting to approach the thought of these matters without harshness, as is common to all who have chosen godliness, having set before them the goal, for the flesh indeed wages war against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, as it is written (Galatians 5:17).
These things are opposed to one another.
And so we say that every kind of necessity, when the flesh is in some measure corrupted and its motions enfeebled, then the other—namely, the mindset of the Spirit—grows all the more vigorously.
He brings in a recounting of causes and, as it were, a recollection of what was previously said, introducing the 'Therefore'.

He then said: 'Indeed, if we who are alive are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may be made visible in our hearts, and we possess this hope, he says—yes, even to those who are about to come and attain to it—we do not lose heart, for we foresee the beauty of the glory to come; but even if affliction should come upon us, we endure it nobly.'
For if indeed, as mere humans, we suffer pain and endure some bodily harm, yet we are not overcome by these things.
For the inward person of us is being renewed.
And the message is common to all.
Therefore, when to those engaged in the labors of training our outward self is being corrupted, then necessarily our inward self is renewed day by day.

And furthermore, upon the things that have been said, since to Jews and also to Greeks we proclaimed Jesus, they have endured terrible and unbearable persecutions, and their bodies have been worn down by the labors they undertook.
Yet the greater the labor, the more I think it would reasonably follow that the opposition against grace should be met with an even greater supply of divine favor.
For our present, light affliction is working for us an excess upon excess—an eternal weight of glory—while we do not fix our gaze on what is seen, but on what is unseen (2 Corinthians 4:17-18).
For the things seen are temporary, but the things unseen are eternal.

He strengthens those who wish to contend: making the contests seem small, yet lifting up the crowns for the victors; placing the light burden upon our afflictions, but the weighty glory upon the reward.

For those who make measured progress in this life on account of what is temporary, even if it should abound to excess, still they look forward to passing into an eternal weight of glory, because the good things of the age to come surpass mere speech.
Therefore, we must not fix our attention on the seen, temporary things, but on the unseen, eternal ones.
We know that if our earthly tent—the body—is torn down, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (Job 4:19).

For it is written: 'Those who dwell in houses of clay, from the same clay we are.', thus we understand that when death has destroyed our earthly tent, that is our body, it will not be long—according to the evident time of the resurrection—before we receive a heavenly dwelling, that is, immortality itself.
He declares that this dwelling is from above, first of all because the thing needed is God-given.

Moreover, by this very reason, since all those who dwell above in the city—I mean the orders of the holy angels—exist in incorruptible and imperishable bodies, the angelic nature has been released from this earthly thickness.
Therefore, the building from God, the house not made by hands and moreover eternal, he names incorruptibility.
And indeed in this we groan, desiring to put on our dwelling from heaven.
Therefore, we groan as being weighed down by corruption, yet we cling to the things above.
